entries.title: Databricks and SAP unleash end-to-end data & AI capabilities to level up enterprise AI transformation
entries.summary: Today's AI models are more capable than ever. What they still lack is the business...
entries.content:
With the new SAP Application Data Foundation, SAP and Databricks customers gain simpler, more performant access in SAP Databricks to data from SAP applications, across cloud and on-premises.

by Sanjay Chheda, Katie Cummiskey, Patrick Werns, Akram Chetibi and Qi Su

  • Databricks and SAP are expanding their partnership to provide expanded access to SAP application data across cloud and on-premises to accelerate time to value for advanced analytics and AI.
  • New Databricks capabilities including Genie, Lakeflow, Unity Gateway, and Lakebase come to SAP Databricks fully integrated with SAP Business Data Cloud.
  • Customers can put all their SAP data to work with the full range of the Databricks Data + AI Platform and AI capabilities.

Today's AI models are more capable than ever. What they still lack is the business context to understand how your company actually runs. For most enterprises, that context lives in SAP systems. Over 90% of Fortune 500 companies use SAP solutions to manage key business processes, enhance operational efficiency, and gain a competitive edge through data-driven decision-making.

Last year, SAP and Databricks introduced SAP Databricks, which natively embedded the Databricks Data + AI Platform in SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC). Since general availability, customers including Adidas, Zalando, Mondi, and CAF have used SAP Databricks and SAP BDC Connect for Databricks to analyze, govern, and build AI on live, semantically rich SAP Data Products through zero-copy, bi-directional OpenSharing.

This week at SAP TechEd, we are announcing the next phase of our partnership. Now, we’re bringing together the expanded scope of Databricks to SAP Databricks in SAP Business Data Cloud. This makes it much easier and more performant to work with SAP enterprise data, allowing customers to realize AI value from their data.

Customers want to put their data to work: forecasting demand from years of order history, detecting anomalies in the financial close, optimizing procurement decisions, and grounding AI agents in how the business actually runs. Accessing SAP application data has been possible, but it has typically meant building and maintaining custom extraction pipelines that copy data, lose business context along the way, and fragment governance.

As SAP announced at TechEd, SAP Application Data Foundation makes data from SAP applications available for consumption in the SAP Business Data Cloud engine of choice, including SAP Databricks. It provides a cloud-native way to access SAP application data, helping to lower total cost of ownership and reduce time to value. For SAP Databricks customers, that means:

  • No more custom extraction pipelines: SAP data products can be shared with SAP BDC Connect for zero-copy access, avoiding additional pipelines, data copies and silos.
  • AI built on SAP business semantics: Data engineers can build models on a semantically rich foundation, so analytics and AI reflect how the business actually runs.
  • The full Databricks Data + AI Platform on SAP data: Genie, Lakeflow, Unity Gateway and Lakebase turn that data into enriched data products, apps and agents.

For example, a manufacturer running finance and supply chain on SAP ECC on-premises, while planning its move to the cloud, can use SAP Application Data Foundation to bring years of order history into SAP Databricks. Its data engineers can enrich that history with third-party data and build demand-forecasting models on SAP's business semantics, without custom extraction pipelines, and keep that work as they move to the cloud.

The expanded partnership plans to bring the full range of Databricks data and enterprise AI capabilities to SAP Databricks, embedded within SAP BDC.

  • Genie: An AI coworker that gives every team instant access to governed data and AI, with enterprise context built in. Genie delivers the context in core SAP data to every team and agent. A planned bi-directional integration between Genie and Joule can bring those answers and actions into SAP experiences.
  • Lakeflow: A unified data engineering solution to ingest, transform, and orchestrate data, so teams can build pipelines that combine SAP data with IoT, CRM, and third-party sources.
  • Unity Gateway: Multi-AI governance and cost control across agents, tools, models, and MCPs, so teams can scale AI on SAP data with guardrails and spend controls in place.
  • Lakebase: The first serverless, mission-critical Postgres database built for AI apps and agents that helps teams build operational data apps on SAP and enterprise data.
  • One place to govern data and AI. Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway govern data, models, and agents across SAP and non-SAP data.
  • Choice of architecture. Customers can use SAP data inside SAP BDC with SAP Databricks or bring governed SAP data or data products they create based on SAP data into an existing Databricks estate, with any model on any cloud.
  • Faster time to value. SAP and Databricks are expanding our go-to-market partnership, with joint teams in the field so joint customers can accelerate their AI transformation based on critical enterprise data helping customers get value faster.
“Data is the foundation for enterprise AI. By bringing the latest scope of Databricks into SAP Business Data Cloud, we’re combining SAP’s deep understanding of business processes and mission-critical applications and agents with Databricks’ industry-leading data platform. With that, we help customers turn their enterprise data into a powerful foundation for the Autonomous Enterprise.” - Philipp Herzig, Chief Technology Officer, SAP SE
"This partnership brings together the most critical business data in the enterprise, SAP data, with the leading Data + AI Platform, Databricks. With the new SAP Application Data Foundation and SAP Databricks in BDC, companies can finally bring all of their SAP data together and unleash the full capabilities of the Databricks platform to drive business insights. They can also combine Genie with Joule to deliver that business context to every team and agent so they can get trusted answers and act on them."- Michael Kiermaier, SVP Business Strategy and Operations, Databricks

SAF-Holland, a global manufacturer of chassis components for trailers, trucks, and buses, uses SAP BDC and SAP Databricks to unify more than 100 million records of customer, delivery, and material data. The company applies machine learning to predict the reliability of customer delivery schedules. SAF-Holland now generates analyses 5x faster than with traditional reporting approaches, and turns complex SAP data into planning and supply chain insights in minutes instead of weeks.

"Opening the SAP data ecosystem to Databricks has unlocked better analysis for our internal teams and ultimately helps us deliver better outcomes for our customers."- David Gund, Senior Manager of Global Digital Intelligence, SAF-Holland

SAP Databricks and SAP Business Data Cloud Connect for Databricks are available today. Talk to your SAP or Databricks account team to learn about the new SAP Application Data Foundation and expanded SAP Databricks capabilities and plan your path to analytics and AI on all your SAP data.

entries.content:
How governed case context connects evidence, supervised agents, and human judgment to move clients from first document to funded account.

  • Task-level AI speeds up document processing and KYC screening, but wealth management client onboarding still stalls when evidence, case state, and decisions remain fragmented across systems.
  • Governed case context gives AI agents and human reviewers a shared, versioned view of each case, including its evidence, exceptions and decision history.
  • On Databricks Data + AI Platform, supervised AI agents coordinate the full journey with governance, traceability, and human oversight. Measure the impact through cycle time, manual touches, and approval-to-funding time.

Wealth Management client onboarding can stall even when every system has done its job. The document is collected, the screening result is back, and the workflow task is complete. Yet the case is still waiting because someone has to determine what changed, which evidence is current, and who owns the exception.

For the client, those boundaries are invisible. They experience one journey and expect their information and progress to move with them. Inside the firm, however, that journey crosses customer relationship management (CRM), document, know your customer (KYC), screening, custody, and workflow systems, each holding a different part of the case.

Firms have invested in making those individual steps faster, and AI is accelerating them further. But a quicker extraction, screening summary, or routing decision does little if the next team must still reconstruct the case, reconcile the evidence, and reopen work that appeared complete.

Onboarding still loses time at these handoffs. A modern platform has to connect the case across systems, coordinate work as conditions change, and preserve the controls and human judgment that the process depends on. When it doesn't, the cost accumulates between systems.

The first cost is what clients feel most directly: time.

In Singapore, opening a private banking account takes about 6 weeks, with complex cases taking longer. In May 2026, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said initiatives from an account-opening workgroup co-led by MAS and industry were expected to bring that median within one month.

Inside the firm, it shows up in staff time. The Capgemini World Wealth Report 2026 found that 60% of 144 wealth executives lacked a unified client view. The same report found that 1,317 relationship managers across 16 markets said operational work consumed 41% of their time. That figure covers wealth operations broadly, not onboarding alone, but it shows how much capacity routine coordination can absorb.

The onboarding journey itself spans many teams. A 2024 EY report of more than a dozen global asset managers found that more than half involved at least 10 teams in onboarding. Yet only 15% reported strong integration with their CRM systems.

“More than half of global asset managers involve at least 10 teams in onboarding, yet only 15% report strong CRM integration.”

A 2024 KPMG and Private Wealth Management Association study of 35 Hong Kong private wealth institutions cited onboarding demands as a factor in rising costs and deteriorating client experience.

The findings span markets, populations, and supervisory regimes, and each needs to be read in context. Across them, the pattern is consistent - fragmented client information, with many teams stitching the journey together.

Firms absorb that coordination through staff hours, repeated evidence searches, manual reconciliation, exception handling, and control-history preparation. Integration, maintenance, and change testing add more cost while account opening and funding wait.

Faster tasks do not always produce a faster onboarding journey. A system can finish its work on time and still leave the case stalled at the next handoff.

AI can accelerate each task further, but it does not automatically remove friction between systems.

AI is already moving into wealth and asset management. In a 2025 EY survey of 100 decision-makers, split evenly between wealth and asset management firms, 95% of firms reported scaling generative AI across multiple use cases, while 78% were exploring agentic AI. Yet translating this momentum into measurable business value remains a challenge, with only 27% of executives reporting substantial business impact from GenAI.

Looking at the work itself explains the gap. AI can extract document fields, summarize a screening result, or recommend the next workflow action. Each capability may improve a task within a single application, yet the handoff still depends on current evidence and a clear record of what changed. Teams also need to know whether earlier work must be revisited.

AI agents make that dependency more important because routing work across specialist agents and approved tools requires a shared case state. That state must show what is complete, what has gone stale, and which exception blocks the next step. Without it, faster orchestration can reproduce the same fragmentation it was meant to reduce.

Governed case context is a current, versioned, source-linked view of each client onboarding case. It brings together the evidence, case state, completed controls, open exceptions, agent activity, and decision history. Because the context is versioned, teams can see what changed, what the change affected and whether earlier work needs to be revisited.

Different parts of onboarding can live in different places. Core client and custody records may remain in their assigned systems, while evidence processing, controls, models, and case workflows can run on the Databricks Data + AI Platform. Governed case context connects that work in one governed view, as the diagram below illustrates, while preserving record ownership and decision authority. On Databricks, Unity Catalog centralizes access controls, lineage and auditability for this context, while open table formats such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg support reliable data management and interoperability across systems.

Governed case context is useful only when it helps the next agent or reviewer understand and advance the case. A practical test is whether they can answer four questions without reconstructing its history:

  • What evidence is current, and which source and version support it?
  • What work is complete, what has changed and which results may now be stale?
  • What remains unresolved, and what is the next permitted action?
  • Which work can an agent or approved tool perform, and where must an authorized reviewer decide?

With those answers in one place, a governed supervisor agent can resume work from the current case state. It can assign independent tasks to specialist agents, call approved tools, and bring in a reviewer when judgment is required. It can also flag conflicting evidence and assemble a complete package for review, while the evidence, changes, and actions behind that package remain attached to the case.

The value comes from putting this context to work across the journey. A modern platform must keep it current, coordinate agents and people around it, and preserve visibility and governance from the first piece of evidence through the final decision.

Putting governed case context to work requires four platform capabilities. Together, they address the friction identified earlier: rebuilding the case at each handoff, coordinating work manually, governing access to sensitive data, and measuring tasks without seeing the whole journey.

  • Maintain a current view of the case:

    As evidence arrives, controls run and decisions are made, the platform should update the governed context and preserve its links to the underlying sources. Systems assigned to particular records can remain authoritative, while agents and teams work from the same versioned context. On Databricks, Lakeflow Connect brings changes from supported source systems into the platform, Databricks AI Functions extract and classify new evidence and Lakebase maintains the live transactional state used by onboarding applications.

  • Coordinate agent work while people retain authority:

    A governed supervisor agent should select the next permitted action based on the current case state, sending defined tasks to specialist agents or approved tools and bringing in a qualified reviewer when judgment is required. People retain responsibility for exceptions, overrides and onboarding approval. On Databricks, Supervisor Agents can coordinate specialist agents and approved tools, including Unity Catalog functions, MCP services and Genie Agents (formerly Spaces), over governed enterprise data.

  • Govern data, tools and actions:

    Onboarding involves personally identifiable information (PII) and other sensitive records. Each agent should have access only to the data and tools required for its task, with sensitive fields masked or withheld where appropriate. Agent activity should remain traceable and reviewable. On Databricks, Unity Catalog provides fine-grained access controls, masking, lineage and auditability across governed data and AI assets, while Unity Gateway extends that governance to agent runtime by controlling which models and MCP tools each agent can call, applying guardrails, routing requests across models, enforcing budgets and rate limits, and logging every request.

  • Measure end to end:

    Teams should monitor agent quality, latency, reliability and escalation alongside cycle time, manual touches, rework, exceptions and approval-to-funding time. The operating picture should also include integration changes, duplicated data movement and the effort required to prepare control evidence. Databricks Apps can embed Databricks AI/BI dashboards within the queue and case workspace, giving operations and compliance leaders a consolidated view of journey performance alongside active cases.

Together, these capabilities turn governed case context into an operating model. The architecture below shows how the context, supervised agents, and human review work together in practice.

The architecture puts the four capabilities into a recurring operating loop around each case. Information can arrive from source systems, while evidence processing, controls, risk models, and onboarding workflows run on the platform. Each result returns to governed case context with its source references and history attached, giving the next agent or reviewer the current state of the case.

A governed supervisor agent reads that context and selects the next permitted action. Depending on the case, it can call an approved tool, assign work to a specialist agent, or involve a reviewer. When new evidence makes an earlier result stale, it can reopen the affected work instead of restarting the entire case. It also monitors completion and freshness, flagging missing or conflicting control results before the case moves forward.

A simple example shows how the loop works. Consider a case waiting on a required document. The supervisor can identify the gap, prepare a client outreach email for review and pause any work that depends on the missing evidence. Once a reviewer approves the outreach and the document arrives through the designated channel, the case context updates. The supervisor can then trigger document processing, rerun only the affected checks and route the case to its next permitted step.

In this illustrative design, each specialist agent has a defined job:

  • A document intelligence agent reads submitted files, extracts the required information, and flags missing evidence.
  • A KYC and screening agent brings together results from identity, KYC, and screening controls.
  • A risk analysis agent evaluates verified case facts against defined rules and control results.
  • A case summary agent prepares a draft assessment for review.

Each result returns to governed case context with its supporting evidence and source references. The supervisor uses that updated state to determine whether another agent should act, human review is required, or the case can move forward.

People retain decision authority. From a controlled workspace, reviewers can inspect evidence, request additional information, resolve an exception, record an override with its rationale or make a decision within their authority. Their actions become part of the case history and may trigger another agent task or a targeted rerun. Case Recommendation remains a draft assessment. Alert disposition, risk acceptance, and onboarding approval remain with the systems and reviewers assigned that authority.

Governance follows the work through the entire loop. Fine-grained access limits each agent to the data and tools required for its job. Agent traces record what each agent did, how long it took and its estimated model cost. Teams can use that history to evaluate quality, spot regressions and investigate failures. These traces support AI and model-risk oversight, while authorized decisions remain in the business record. Together, traces and decision records give compliance and audit teams a reconstructable account of each case: what evidence was reviewed, which controls ran, what each agent produced, and who approved, overrode or escalated the outcome, and why. That record supports AML/KYC record-keeping and exam readiness, because firms can show how each decision was reached instead of piecing the history together after the fact.

The reviewer workspace records human actions, while the application maintains the live case state required by the workflow. After an authorized decision, a controlled integration records the approved outcome in the system assigned to own it. On Databricks, the reviewer workspace can run as a Databricks App, with Lakebase maintaining the live case state.

The value of this operating model must be measured across the entire journey, from the first evidence collected through account funding. Otherwise, a faster agent or control may simply move the delay to the next handoff.

The architecture creates value when it improves the whole onboarding journey. Faster agent responses matter, but the real test is whether cases move sooner, teams spend less time coordinating work, and controls remain effective.

Start with one high-friction path. Choose an onboarding journey where handoffs, rework and delays are already visible. Before the pilot begins, align wealth operations, compliance, data, and technology leaders. Agree on the required evidence, who owns each record and decision, where human judgment is mandatory, and which actions the supervisor may trigger.

Establish the baseline before changing the workflow. Measure the current journey across three areas:

  • Cost and capacity: Cost per completed onboarding and the advisor, operations, and compliance hours spent on each case.
  • Journey performance: Median and 90th-percentile cycle time, approval-to-funding time, manual touches, systems accessed, document rework, exceptions, incomplete cases, and abandonment.
  • Technology and control: The cost of running and changing integrations, duplicated data movement and the effort required to assemble control, lineage and audit evidence.

Together, these measures surface work that often disappears inside team queues and system handoffs. They also show whether governed case context has reduced repeated reconciliation and evidence searches or simply moved the work elsewhere.

Set the success thresholds before the pilot begins. Evaluate speed, staff effort, agent quality, trace completeness and control effectiveness. The supervisor and specialist agents should reduce avoidable handoffs and prepare a more complete case for review. Their traces should make the work easier to evaluate and investigate.

Exception, override and reopened-case rates still require root-cause and quality review. An increase could indicate a control problem. It could also mean the new process is detecting issues that were previously missed.

Read the results across the journey:

  • If median cycle time improves while the 90th percentile does not, complex cases are still getting stuck.
  • If agent processing speeds up while approval-to-funding time remains unchanged, the bottleneck has shifted.
  • If manual touches fall while control-evidence preparation stays flat, the final review package still needs work.

Scale when the gains hold from first evidence collected through account funding and control effectiveness remains intact. The standard for modern onboarding is straightforward: move the case faster, make every agent action reviewable and preserve human authority wherever judgment matters.

Faster document processing, screening, or routing does not resolve fragmented evidence, case state, and decision history. Onboarding can still stall at the next handoff when teams must determine what changed, which work remains valid, and who should act.

Governed case context is a current, source-linked and versioned view of an onboarding case. It connects evidence, case state, control results, exceptions, agent activity and decision history so agents and reviewers can work from the same context.

A governed supervisor agent can route work across specialist agents for document intelligence, KYC screening, and risk analysis, and approved tools while involving reviewers when judgment is required. Fine-grained access and traces make agent activity reviewable, while people retain authority over exceptions, overrides and onboarding approval.

No. Core records may remain in CRM, custody, or other assigned systems, while evidence processing, controls, models, and workflows run on the Databricks Data + AI platform, with Unity Catalog governing data, models, and agent tools. Governed case context connects the work while preserving record ownership and decision authority.

Firms should measure results across the entire onboarding journey rather than relying on agent speed alone. Useful measures include cycle time, approval-to-funding time, manual touches, rework, staff effort, integration cost and control effectiveness. Firms should scale when improvements hold end to end and agent actions remain reviewable.

Start with one high-friction onboarding journey and measure the impact from first evidence through account funding. See how Databricks helps financial services firms build governed, traceable agentic workflows with people in control.

entries.title: Deliberate decisions and enterprise AI value
entries.summary: AI progress is moving quickly. Expectations are rising, experimentation is spreading...
entries.content:
Discover how senior data and AI leaders are balancing momentum, accountability and flexibility to turn AI ambition into sustained enterprise value.

by Jack Yallop and Lexy Kassan

  • Why AI progress needs grounded decisions when readiness, evidence and expectations are uneven.
  • What senior leaders are learning about investment, ownership, human judgment and strategic flexibility.
  • How 5 leadership disciplines help turn AI ambition into sustained enterprise value.

AI progress is moving quickly. Expectations are rising, experimentation is spreading and organizations are under pressure to show meaningful returns. But the decisions that matter most are rarely about whether AI is possible. They are about where to commit, what to prioritize and how to move forward when the evidence is still incomplete.

That is the focus of Deliberate Decisions: How Grounded Leadership Is Advancing the Path to Enterprise AI Value, a report produced by DataIQ in partnership with Databricks. The report brings together perspectives from senior data and AI leaders who are making these choices in real organizations.

The report draws on open peer discussions at DataIQ Guild 2026, an invite-only think tank for senior data and AI leaders. Across industries, leaders described a similar challenge: they are expected to maintain momentum while technology, operating models, workforce impact and business cases continue to evolve.

Early AI success can raise expectations faster than an organization can absorb. Pilots and proofs of concept can multiply before teams have the capacity to assess, govern and support them. Ownership can become unclear as AI crosses functions, while roles and workflows change faster than organizations can define them.

The answer is not to slow down until everything is certain. Nor is it to commit to every promising use case. The report points toward a more grounded form of leadership: making deliberate, evidence-based choices while preserving the ability to adapt.

Report snapshot:

  • Two days of peer discussion at DataIQ Guild 2026 underpin the report.
  • Five recurring pressures are shaping the current data and AI environment.
  • Five leadership disciplines emerged to help leaders respond deliberately.
  • Four stages describe the AI adoption journey: concerned, curious, comfortable and competent.

Download the report now: Deliberate Decisions: How Grounded Leadership Is Advancing the Path to Enterprise AI Value

Five leadership disciplines emerged from the discussions at DataIQ Guild 2026:

  • Confidence grounded in reality: test AI progress against evidence, readiness and the realities of production.
  • Enterprise choices, not demand-led reactions: prioritize business outcomes over isolated enthusiasm or use-case volume.
  • Leadership through influence, not control: create clarity, ownership and proportionate governance across the enterprise.
  • Human judgment as a strategic capability: preserve the authority, context and skills people need to challenge AI outputs.
  • Stability without rigidity: anchor purpose, decision rights and standards while keeping roles and technology choices flexible.

To lead data and AI today is to navigate a constant tension between commitment and flexibility. Every investment, architecture and operating model decision requires leaders to balance confidence in what they know today with openness to what may change tomorrow.

The Databricks perspective in the report identifies four foundations for navigating that tension:

  • Context grounds AI in trusted, governed data.
  • Control gives leaders confidence that innovation can progress responsibly and securely.
  • Cost keeps sustainable adoption aligned with ambition and efficiency.
  • Choice preserves the ability to evolve as technologies, models and business priorities change.

These foundations are reflected in Databricks capabilities such as Lakebase, a governed transactional foundation for building and running data and AI applications and agents, and Genie, which helps people and AI agents access organizational context responsibly and efficiently.

Together, they reinforce the report’s central message: progress does not require waiting for certainty. It requires making informed decisions, knowing where to commit and preserving choice.

A successful pilot is not the same as an AI capability that is ready for production. The report explores the difference between early results and sustainable adoption, including the operational support, governance, skills, monitoring and cost model that become visible once AI enters a live workflow. As Thomas Gebetsroither, Data & Analytics Operations Lead, Axpo Trading & Sales, mentioned:

“The cost is not just the model or the tool. It is the security, the support, the adoption, the governance and the operating model around it. If those costs are invisible, the business case is incomplete.”

Leaders will find a practical way to test whether an AI initiative can remain useful, reliable and affordable beyond the conditions of a bounded experiment.

AI demand can come from the board, business functions, employees and vendors. But demand alone cannot determine the agenda. The report looks at how leaders start with a well-defined business problem, make trade-offs visible and prioritize work with enterprise-scale potential.

It also examines why AI investment may be better managed as a portfolio. Organizations can make a range of initial bets, increase investment as evidence strengthens and stop or redirect work that does not justify further commitment.

“Not every investment needs to pay back in the same way. Some will deliver direct value, some will generate learning and some will create capabilities that can be reused across the organisation.”- Gavin Goodland, Chief Data Officer, National Grid

AI adoption is not owned by one team. Business outcomes, workflow change, risk, adoption and ongoing costs are distributed across the organization. You will learn why clear decision rights are not enough unless a business owner is also prepared to own the outcome and its consequences.

This matters because an approved use case without committed ownership can create a new problem rather than solve an existing one.

“We want the business to be accountable. Any of the use cases that we get prioritized need to have an impact on the long-range plan.”- Bharathi Rajan, VP – Data, Digital & AI, Swire Coca-Cola

As AI handles more execution, people spend more time framing problems, interpreting results and deciding what happens next. The report examines why human authority must be explicit, how organizations can build role-appropriate AI fluency and why automating away opportunities to develop expertise can create long-term risk.

The central question is not whether humans remain somewhere in the process. It is whether they still have the authority, context and time to challenge an output when it matters.

Organizations need enough continuity to know where accountability sits and which principles apply. At the same time, technology choices, roles and operating models need room to evolve. As the report delineates, the challenge for leaders is not to protect people from automation. It is to avoid automating away capabilities the organisation cannot replace.

The report offers a way to identify the fixed points that matter — purpose, decision rights, standards, human authority and business ownership — while keeping other decisions flexible and, where possible, reversible.

Deliberate Decisions does not predict which technology will win. It focuses on the judgment calls leaders are making now: what to commit to, where to push back, how to move forward responsibly and how to preserve choice as conditions change.

For leaders moving from experimentation toward enterprise AI value, the report provides a practical framework and shared language for making trade-offs visible. Rather than presenting a use case as an isolated technical project, connect it to the business outcome it should change, the evidence supporting the next investment and the ownership required to sustain it.

That creates more useful conversations with executive sponsors and business teams. It also makes it easier to assess readiness, stop, redirect, or redesign work when the evidence changes, treating course correction as disciplined leadership rather than failure.

Before approving the next use case, ask:

  • What evidence shows that this capability is ready for the conditions of the live enterprise?
  • Who owns the outcome, including adoption, operating consequences and ongoing cost?
  • Which parts of this decision should remain flexible if technology, roles or business priorities change?

These questions will not remove uncertainty. They can improve the quality of the decisions made in its presence.

The full report develops these ideas through five leadership disciplines and perspectives from the DataIQ Guild community. It is designed to help leaders compare their own decisions with the choices other organizations are making as AI becomes more consequential.

Download the full Deliberate Decisions report to explore the leadership model and the practical actions behind it.

Look beyond pilot results. AI is ready to scale when the organization can support, govern, adopt and afford it in a live workflow.

Start with a clearly defined business problem and enterprise value. Manage initiatives as a portfolio, increasing investment as evidence strengthens.

A business owner should be accountable for the outcome, adoption, operating consequences and ongoing costs, with clear decision rights across teams.

Define which decisions remain human-owned and give people the authority, context and time to challenge, override or stop an AI system.

Set fixed points for purpose, standards, ownership and human authority, while keeping roles, operating models and technology choices open to review.

entries.title: Announcing General Availability of Real-Time Mode for Spark Declarative Pipelines on Databricks
entries.summary: We introduced Real-Time Mode (RTM) last year which enabled customers to build low-latency, operational use cases...
entries.content:
Bring sub-second latency to your most time-critical operational workloads with declarative flows and sinks

by Jerry Peng, Abhay Bothra, Sudhanva Huruli, Navneeth Nair, Anant Pingle and Murali Talluri

  • Announcing General Availability of Real-Time Mode (RTM) on Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP), delivering end-to-end processing latencies in the millisecond range for operational streaming workloads.
  • Real-Time Mode eliminates the need for separate specialized engines such as Apache Flink, unifying batch, ETL, and low-latency streaming under a single framework.
  • Real-Time Mode enables real-time computation and instant writes to operational stores via ForEach sinks, powering time-critical use cases like fraud detection and live personalization.

We introduced Real-Time Mode (RTM) last year which enabled customers to build low-latency, operational use cases. This was a game changer because it allowed customers to process streaming data in milliseconds, up to 100x faster than traditional micro-batch architecture. Furthermore, they no longer needed to maintain separate, specialized engines like Flink alongside Spark, eliminating duplicate codebases, fragmented governance models, and operational overhead.

Today, we are announcing RTM in Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP) is now Genearally Available. SDP has become the standard way to build streaming and ETL pipelines on Databricks, automatically handling dependency resolution, incremental processing, orchestration, failure recovery, and data quality enforcement. With RTM, customers can build operational, low-latency pipelines while retaining all of those SDP benefits. Whether for fraud scoring, real-time alerting, or pushing fresh features to operational stores, you can now use SDP across all of these use cases.

RTM is an evolution of the Spark Structured Streaming engine that achieves end-to-end latencies in the millisecond range. It does this by streaming data continuously, running all query stages simultaneously, and passing data between stages as soon as it is produced. For the full architecture deep dive, read the blog, “Breaking the microbatch barrier: The architecture of Apache Spark Real-Time Mode.”

RTM can support any workload that benefits from turning data into decisions in milliseconds. Some example use cases include fraud detection, live personalization, real-time recommendation systems, and real-time feature computation. We benchmarked RTM against Apache Flink on actual customer workloads performing feature computation, and RTM is up to 92% faster than specialized engines like Flink. Below are the benchmarks. For more information on the datasets and queries referenced, see this GitHub repository.

Customers are increasingly defaulting to SDP for their ETL workloads. With RTM, SDP now supports all streaming workloads, including operational low-latency streaming, enabling customers to use a single framework across all pipelines. One framework means one observability stack, one billing model, and no fragmentation across different APIs.

SDP serverless takes it further. There is no compute to choose and no cluster to size. You get sub-second latency, without any complex infra tuning, while paying only for the cores your query uses. RTM flows also get SDP features such as versionless upgrades and low-downtime maintenance, which reduce both the operational work and the disruption of upgrades.

One use case where RTM on SDP has immediate impact is real-time feature computation. ML models for fraud detection or personalization depend on fresh signals, such as a user's total transaction amount over the last 10 minutes, to make accurate predictions. Computing these rolling-window aggregations and landing them in an online store within milliseconds is where RTM on SDP closes the gap. The Databricks Feature Store uses this exact architecture to deliver end-to-end p99 latency of 200ms from Kafka to the online feature store.

Real-Time Mode requires the pipeline mode to be 

continuous
and 
spark.databricks.streaming.realTimeMode.enabled
set to 
true
takes over.

Real-time mode requires an update flow. Use 

dp.create_sink()
to define the output target, then use the 
@dp.update_flow
decorator with 
pipelines.trigger
set to 
"RealTime"
and 
target
pointing to the sink.

For supported sources and sinks, see the documentation.

Use cases like fraud detection or real-time personalization require not only that features be computed in real time but also that they land in a queryable, low-latency store. A fraud model needs a customer's latest transaction before it clears, and a personalization engine needs to read what a user just browsed.

Today, you can write to any custom sink like Lakebase, Redis, or any other OLTP store from SDP using a ForEach sink. Define the writer, register it as a 

foreach_sink
, and wire it to an 
update_flow
.

Features land in your operational store within milliseconds of being produced, with no offline-to-online sync in between. Applications and models can query them at ultra-low latency. 

What’s next for RTM on serverless?

  • Running RTM pipelines at lower cost: Bin-pack multiple RTM flows into a single pipeline instead of each query standing up its own resources. The system also auto-tunes source and shuffle partitions based on workload, so users skip manual sizing.
  • Expanded sink support: Native Lakebase sink for SDP, with built-in batching, automatic retries, and UC-managed authentication.

RTM extends Spark Declarative Pipelines into a new class of workloads, operational, latency-sensitive applications that demand immediate response to streaming data. By bringing sub-second latency to the SDP APIs your team already uses, it eliminates the need to operate a separate framework or engine for your most time-critical pipelines. Whether you're building fraud detection pipelines, personalization engines, or ML feature computation systems, real-time mode gives you the latency your application demands with the simplicity of SDP.

Real-Time Mode on Spark Declarative Pipelines is now Generally Available.

Check out the following resources to get started with RTM on SDP:

  • Documentation: Use Real-Time Mode on Lakeflow pipelines
  • Documentation: Connect to Lakebase streaming sink
  • Documentation: Use a ForEach sink to write each row in pipelines
  • Code examples: Real-Time Mode on SDP examples

What is Real-Time Mode (RTM) in Spark Declarative Pipelines?

Real-time mode (RTM) lets Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP) process streaming data with end-to-end latency in the millisecond range. It streams data continuously, runs all query stages at the same time and passes data between stages as soon as it's produced. Real-time pipelines benefit from SDP's orchestration and automatic failure recovery.

Is Real-Time Mode available in Spark Declarative Pipelines?

Yes. Real-time mode on Spark Declarative Pipelines is now generally available. It brings the real-time mode already available in Spark Structured Streaming to SDP pipelines.

How do I turn on real-time mode in a pipeline?

Set the pipeline to 

continuous
mode and set 
spark.databricks.streaming.realTimeMode.enabled
to 
true
. Then define an update flow with 
pipelines.trigger
set to 
"RealTime"
and a target that points to a sink.

Can a real-time pipeline write to Lakebase or another OLTP store?

Yes. Define a ForEach sink with a writer that implements 

open
, 
process
and 
close
, then point a real-time flow at it. This works for Lakebase, Redis or any other OLTP store.

What use cases is Real-Time Mode in Spark Declarative Pipelines built for?

Real-Time Mode is built for operational workloads that turn streaming data into decisions in milliseconds. Examples include fraud detection, live personalization, real-time recommendations and real-time feature computation. The Databricks feature store uses this architecture to reach a p99 latency of 200 ms from Apache Kafka to the online feature store.

entries.title: Smarter cost controls for serverless
entries.summary: At Databricks, our serverless compute usage has grown more than 3x in the past year,...
entries.content:
Bringing familiar cost controls to serverless compute

by Piyush Singh and Vijay Raja

  • Serverless cost controls now go beyond infrastructure settings to who can run workloads, how costs are attributed, and how much they can spend.
  • Teams can already take action today with usage-policy tags, billing system tables, access controls and budget alerts.
  • Rate limits, now available, along with shared budgets (coming soon) help prevent runaway workloads and keep team spending within bounds.

At Databricks, our serverless compute usage has grown more than 3x in the past year, and thousands of customers now run mission critical notebooks, jobs, and pipelines on it. As adoption climbs, the question every platform team asks first only gets louder: how do we gain better visibility into serverless costs and keep the cost within our budget?

Databricks customers running serverless SQL and Model Serving already attribute spend, govern access, and monitor consumption without touching a single cluster knob. We are now bringing that same functionality to serverless compute for notebooks, jobs, and pipelines. We are making serverless cost controls work the way platform teams already expect it to.

On classic compute, cost control lived in the infrastructure. You capped spend by capping machines: node counts, instance types, autoscaling ranges, and cluster policies that fenced in what users could provision. The controls were required because you had to manage the infrastructure on your own.

Serverless takes those knobs away, on purpose. Provisioning, scaling, and right-sizing infrastructure is the platform's burden now, handled by Databricks, which is a big part of the value. But cost control has to live somewhere, so it moves up a layer. Instead of attaching to machines, it attaches to people and workloads. Who is allowed to run serverless, how fast a workload is allowed to spend, and where the cost lands are the questions that matter now.

Platform teams describe their needs three ways:

  • Runaway spend: a single unbounded notebook run can spend thousands in a day, because there is no cluster size or autoscaling ceiling to bound it.
  • The wrong hands: serverless is available to everyone by default, including users who should not be provisioning it, with no entitlement to gate who can run it.
  • No accountability: teams will not adopt serverless without the tag enforcement they had on classic compute.

Classic compute answered these with three tools: tags to attribute cost, entitlements to control access, and cluster size limits to cap spend. Serverless needs the same three. Two of them exist today, and the third is coming.

  • Attribute costs: know which team, project, or user a serverless DBU belongs to.
  • Control access: decide who can run serverless in the first place, and on what.
  • Limit spend: bound how much/how fast a workload or a team can spend, before the fact, rather than after.

We will dive into each of these in order.

Attribution starts with tags. On classic compute you tagged the cluster; on serverless you tag the compute, and every DBU that compute runs carries that tag through to billing.

  • Serverless Compute Tags: tag a serverless compute object once, and the workloads that run on it are attributed to the right team, project, or cost center, with no separate policy object to maintain.
  • System tables: every serverless DBU lands in 
    system.billing.usage
    , broken out by user, by product, and by tag. A leadership-ready "cost by team" view is a single query, and the account-console cost dashboards render it for you without writing any SQL at all.

The same table answers the audit question you will want before you change anyone's access: who is actually running serverless today, and how much are they spending? That is one more query, ranked by consumption, and the full examples live in the system tables documentation.

Availability: Serverless Compute tags for attribution is currently available in Beta.

Observability is already available and customers can already monitor serverless cost with system tables on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

The same system tables that attribute cost also let you track it. Account-console budgets raise email alerts when serverless spend crosses a threshold, and the cost management dashboards let you track consumption by product, workspace, and tag. A SQL alert on yesterday's serverless spend closes the loop within hours.

Monitoring is reactive, though: it reports the expensive day the next morning rather than preventing it. That gap is why the next two objectives exist.

Availability: Monitoring is generally available today. Set up budgets and spend alerts on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

The first proactive control is deciding who can run serverless at all. That grant is an entitlement: it defines which users or groups can access serverless, just like existing entitlements control who can create clusters or connect to a SQL warehouse. Serverless Compute Access Controls is now generally available and lets you govern serverless with that model: permissions on a compute object, not policies bolted onto every workload.

A serverless compute object is the permission boundary for serverless. Every workspace gets two by default:

  • Default Serverless Interactive Compute: notebooks and Databricks Connect.
  • Default Serverless Automated Compute: jobs and Spark Declarative Pipelines.

Permissions on these objects are the two you already know from warehouses: Can Use and Can Manage. If you can reason about who can attach to a SQL warehouse, you can reason about who can run serverless.

The model is safe by default. Every user starts with Can Use, so turning the feature on changes nothing until an admin acts. When an admin does act, the flow is the one you would expect: open the Compute page, go to the Serverless tab, open a default compute object, remove "All Users," and add a specific group. A user outside that group now sees Serverless grayed out in the notebook compute selector, and nothing that was already running is interrupted.

Availability: Generally available today. See the docs for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

Access control decides whether a workload runs, not how much it can spend once it does. Closing that gap is the third job - Rate Limits – and it lands on the same compute objects you just saw.

  • Rate limits on automated workloads: per-compute limits, expressed as t-shirt sizes (S, M, L, XL) that bound how much or how fast a job or pipeline can spend rather than only whether it can run. Admins would create custom compute objects and share them per team, giving each team its own limit. This is the classic cluster-policy pattern, ported to serverless.
  • Shared budgets for interactive (coming soon): a per-session cap alone cannot protect a team's budget, because many "Medium" sessions still add up. Our direction is a shared limit for the group, with a per-session maximum as the guardrail underneath it.

Attribution improves at the same time. A new 

serverless_compute_id
in 
system.billing.usage
attributes spend per compute object, so "cost by compute object" becomes as easy as "cost by team."

One clarification for anyone who knows DBSQL t-shirt sizes: for notebooks and jobs the size is a maximum autoscaling ceiling, not a fixed cluster size. Pick XL for a job that only needs Medium, and it is allocated Medium.

Availability: Rate limits are now available in Beta. Enable rate limits through your Databricks preview settings; see the docs for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

Put the three jobs back together:

  • Attribute cost: native tags on serverless compute plus 
    serverless_compute_id
    in system tables, usable in budgets and dashboards.
  • Control access: entitlements on serverless compute objects.
  • Limit spend: rate limits, shared across a group and bounded per workload.

You can start implementing serverless cost controls today. Here is how you can get going:

  • Turn on tag enforcement: tag your serverless compute so that attribution is in place before anything else.
  • Stand up monitoring: add cost dashboards on 
    system.billing.usage
    plus a budget alert on serverless spend.
  • Audit who runs serverless today: so that you know the blast radius before you change access.
  • Decide your access posture: who should be able to run serverless interactive, and who should run automated?
  • Turn on Serverless Compute Access Controls: enable fast, fully managed compute for the groups you choose.

Serverless Compute Access Controls is generally available now. To go deeper on attribution and monitoring today, the system tables (AWS | Azure| GCP) and serverless tagging (AWS | Azure | GCP) documentation is the place to start.

entries.title: How Procore is powering construction analytics with OpenSharing
entries.summary: Connecting an industry built on disconnected dataConstruction runs on data that rarely sits in one place...
entries.content:
A practical look at how OpenSharing enabled Procore Analytics, Procore's business intelligence solution for construction, to double the catalog of extractable data for their customers, across all of their projects, across every major cloud.

  • Procore replaced an API-driven, single-daily-refresh analytics product with OpenSharing on Databricks, lifting the once-a-day refresh ceiling so customers can pull data for their downstream systems and business processes hourly.
  • OpenSharing now distributes hundreds of curated tables, maintaining partitioned access per customer to manage hundreds of thousands of distinct data shares at scale.
  • Doubled data availability for end customers and internal product teams, accelerating new product experiences and giving real estate facility owners, general contractors, and specialty contractors a single trusted view of every job.

Construction runs on data that rarely sits in one place. Information is scattered across platforms, regions, and teams, often locked inside the systems of whichever party generated it. When field data isn't connected to the financial system, that disconnect can hide financial risk. When a project manager, a construction executive thousands of miles away, and a superintendent on the jobsite can't see the same view of a project, decisions get made based on stale or partial information.

Procore, a leading global construction management software provider serving tens of thousands of customers across the U.S., Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and Australia, was built to close those gaps — connecting everyone in construction on a single platform. That means three groups in particular: owners (real estate developers and anyone owning and operating the real estate facility or infrastructure themselves), general contractors who manage projects end to end, and specialty contractors like electricians and plumbers who execute the work in the field.

But connecting data inside Procore is only half the story. Customers also need that data in their own environments, alongside everything else they run the business on (e.g. a general contractor pulling Procore data into Power BI to track workforce and personnel metrics across active jobs, or a customer joining it with their ERP and financial systems to see project execution and cost in one place). That is what Procore Analytics delivers: programmatic access to the connected Procore dataset, pulled into whatever the customer already uses — Power BI, Tableau, Snowflake, BigQuery, their own Databricks workspace, or on-prem SQL Server — for reporting and downstream analysis.

The first generation of Procore Analytics predated OpenSharing entirely. It was built on a SQL Server backend. Data was extracted from Procore’s public APIs and loaded into an Azure database that customers could query.

The architecture worked, but it had a hard ceiling. Refreshes were limited to a single daily run, and even customers who paid for additional refreshes were capped at a maximum of three per day. For construction projects where conditions change by the hour, that lag was the single biggest limiting factor.

API-driven extractions also created cost and reliability problems at scale. Pulling data for tens of thousands of customers through public APIs meant running deep recursive calls, which were expensive, brittle, and prone to timing out or hitting limits.

By the time Procore began designing the next generation of Procore Analytics, Databricks was already powering other parts of the Procore platform. That made OpenSharing a natural fit for the customer-facing extract product as well, with several specific advantages over the old API path.

Operational efficiency. Sharing curated files in place removes the cost, brittleness, and timeout risk of running deep recursive API calls for every customer, the same pressure that capped refresh frequency in Procore Analytics 1.0.

Scale. Procore now can share hundreds of curated tables to each customer, maintaining partitioned access per customer to manage hundreds of thousands of distinct data shares at scale. Some of those companies are running hundreds or thousands of concurrent projects, and every one of them needs a current view of the work.

Reach. Procore's customers run on every major cloud and every IT stack imaginable, from Excel and Power BI to fully built-out Databricks environments. OpenSharing's open protocol meets them all. BI tools like Power BI and Tableau work out of the box, and customers who already run on Databricks get a native Databricks-to-Databricks experience without moving any data. Customers on other warehouses and platforms can consume the same shares using the open OpenSharing client libraries.

Reliability and performance. Customers consume curated, governed data that is already cleaned, modeled, and quality-checked, rather than chaining together API calls and stitching the results.

Security and governance. Sharing runs through Unity Catalog, so every table is governed centrally and access is enforced per user and per project. A general contractor can share project progress with the owner while keeping its own financials private.

Procore built Procore Analytics 2.0 on a medallion architecture inside Databricks. Raw events from the Procore application database and integration events land in the bronze layer untouched. Silver applies cleaning, validation, and data quality checks, producing the confirmed datasets that everything downstream depends on. Gold is where the data is aggregated, optimized, and modeled for analytics.

Bronze, silver, and gold all run across multiple regions so processing happens close to the source data. Gold tables are then pulled from each region into a single primary analytics region, which is where OpenSharing fans the data out to customers.

Two recipient paths. Customers without Databricks generate an OpenSharing token directly inside the Procore application and connect using the open protocol. Customers who do have Databricks add their workspace identifier to receive shares natively through Databricks-to-Databricks sharing.

Automated entitlements. A scheduled job watches for new shares and permission changes, reads each user's permissions out of the Procore application, and reconciles the OpenSharing entitlements accordingly. The result is per-user, per-project enforcement with no manual provisioning, so a general contractor can share project progress with the owner while keeping its own financials private, or share trade-partner-scoped data only with that trade partner.

Granularity and incrementality. Procore shares at the schema, view, table, and partition level. Tables have Change Data Feed enabled, so recipients can choose between consuming a full dataset or only what has changed since the last sync, which matters when individual tables hold millions of records.

A common semantic layer. Because the same gold layer powers both Procore's in-app reporting and the customer extract, the schemas and naming conventions line up across products. A customer who sees a value in the Procore UI gets the same value, with the same name, in their extract.

A predictable change cadence. Shipping data to thousands of downstream customer environments means breaking changes have to be telegraphed carefully. A breaking change is anything that can disrupt a customer's downstream pipeline, like renaming a field, changing a column's data type, or restructuring a table. Procore settled on four breaking-change releases per year with six weeks of advance notice, and twelve non-breaking releases per year with three weeks of notice, aligned with the broader organizational release calendar.

A reorganized data team. The old world had two parallel pipelines, one for analytics, one for in-app reporting, each with its own ingestion, modeling, and governance. The new world consolidates that into one path. A single combined pipeline handles ingestion, landing, modeling, and governance, then fans out to data-domain teams aligned to business areas like finance. Each domain team owns its data end to end and works with the relevant application teams on the nuances of each tool, rather than duplicating that knowledge across separate analytics, reporting, and intelligence teams.

The most tangible business outcome is data availability. While Procore Analytics 1.0 took several years to build out its baseline catalog of available tables and fields with OpenSharing, Procore Analytics 2.0 expanded that catalog to hundreds of tables in less than half the time, effectively doubling the surface area of data customers can extract at scale. That matters because Procore is constantly shipping new capabilities, and every new capability produces data customers want to pull into their own environments. A wider catalog means more of that new functionality is available to customers downstream without one-off integration work.

For end customers, the move to OpenSharing lifted the once-a-day refresh ceiling and reshaped the workday. Customers now schedule refreshes to match the rhythm of their business, and many who pull daily actually pull multiple times per day, on whatever cadence their downstream tools support. A project manager preparing for a major client presentation can take a flurry of last-minute updates from an executive that morning and have the live dashboard reflect them in time for the meeting. In the old model, those nuances had to be explained in the meeting itself.

For internal product teams, a single shared pipeline means a tool team can build a new feature and have its data extractable for customers almost as soon as it ships, instead of waiting months for a parallel analytics pipeline to catch up. Procore expects every gain in tool data availability to translate directly into new product experiences for customers.

Beyond the immediate wins in refresh frequency, scale, and reach, the data architecture Procore built on Databricks and OpenSharing gives customers a governed, continuously available foundation for enterprise-wide reporting and intelligence. Whether a customer is standardizing reporting across every active job, feeding project data into enterprise BI, or building AI on top of it, the value starts the same way: with data that is clean, modeled, governed, and available across every system that needs it.

That is exactly what Procore Analytics 2.0 produces. A single, multi-region gold layer that powers Procore's own application experiences, flows into the products customers build on top of their Procore data, and through OpenSharing and Procore's other data pathways, reaches thousands of construction companies on every major cloud. With that foundation in place, enterprise reporting, analytics, and emerging AI use cases all draw on the same trusted, current source of truth, instead of a series of one-off integrations.

The long-term goal aligns with Procore's mission from day one: to connect everyone in construction on a global platform—giving every team on every project the trusted data they need to build safer, faster, and smarter.

"OpenSharing has helped us increase data availability, which means that everybody in construction, from the executives to the project managers to the folks in the field, has better visibility on the jobs that they do. It's helping them deliver projects on time, on budget, and safely."- Matthew Guptill, Product Manager, Procore Analytics

Building a data product your customers consume in their own tools? OpenSharing gives you one open, governed way to deliver live data across every cloud, region, and platform they run on, with no copies to maintain. See how OpenSharing works, then explore the Databricks Marketplace to share and discover live datasets. Explore OpenSharing 

Put your data to work. Procore Analytics turns your project data into actionable business intelligence, connecting information across every job and delivering it to the tools your teams already use. See how Procore Analytics helps you make faster, more certain decisions across your portfolio. Explore Procore Analytics

entries.title: Voice Agents are here. Context turns them into real customer value.
entries.summary: Why voice, and why nowConsider three moments that happen every day in consumer businesses: At...
entries.content:
How Databricks brings governed context, your business ontology, and fast AI decision making together to tailor every customer conversation in real time.

  • Voice is already changing how customers interact with brands. People who moved from storefronts to websites to apps now expect to simply talk to the companies they buy from, and the same shift is reaching suppliers, drivers, and field teams.
  • Most enterprise AI so far has faced inward. The larger opportunity is in the conversations companies have with customers and partners every day, and each of those conversations can now be captured, understood, and acted on in real time.
  • Any team can build a voice agent that talks back, but value is created only when the agent has context on who is calling. From there, it can adapt to that person, stay within set rules, and get better with every call.
  • On Databricks, the agent's brain sits next to your governed data. Context and ontology ground every answer, fast AI decisions tailor each turn, and every call feeds a learning loop.
  • Getting started is straightforward. Pick one high-volume routine call, measure how well the agent handles it, and use the DIVA blueprint as the starting point for the next one.

Consider three moments that happen every day in consumer businesses:

  • At 6 a.m., a driver running late for a delivery window calls dispatch to move his dock appointment. He’s behind the wheel, so an app isn’t an option. Three other drivers are already on hold, and every minute he waits puts the next delivery at risk.
  • At noon, a drive-thru has four cars in line and one employee on the headset, who is also taking payment and handing out orders. Guests can only order by speaking, so the line moves only as fast as one employee can facilitate orders.
  • In the evening, a storm grounds flights, and stranded travelers call their hotel to hold rooms and push back arrivals. Standing at a gate with a bag in each hand, a phone call is easier and faster than a website. The reservations team has two people and forty calls coming in.

In each of these moments, voice is the fastest or only way the customer can reach the business. So if voice ultimately serves the customer and business need most effectively, why is it so often not available or, in more recent times, executed poorly?

For years, the answer was that voice was too hard to get right. That is no longer true. Synthetic voices now sound natural, a conversation can be turned into text and acted on while the caller is still on the line, and today's voice agents can keep pace with the roughly 200 milliseconds it typically takes people to answer each other in conversation.

What has not caught up is how most companies think about it. Enterprise AI investment has largely faced inward, toward assistants for employees, while the larger opportunity sits in the conversations companies have with customers and partners every day. One of the largest quick-service restaurant brands in the United States is already building toward exactly that, with a voice agent that lets guests add items to their cart, change their order, and check out simply by talking.

Example use cases where voice agents can create value.

Every one of these calls, from the driver moving a dock appointment to the traveler holding a room after a storm, depends on more than understanding speech. To be useful, the agent needs the same context your best employee would have: who is calling, what is already in motion for them, and what it is allowed to do about it.

Most voice agent pilots prove that an agent can hold a conversation. Far fewer prove that it can be trusted with a real customer. Context closes that gap. With it, the agent can adapt to each caller, stay within your rules about what it can see and say, and get better with every call. Without it, even the most natural voice can only give generic answers.

Consider a single call. A loyal customer phones about a late order. The agent already knows who they are, what they ordered, and where the package is. It apologizes, offers a loyalty credit it is authorized to give, and arranges a replacement. If the customer is still frustrated, the agent picks up on it in the moment and decides, in a fraction of a second, to route the call to the next available person. That person picks up with the full context, so the customer neither waits in a queue nor repeats themselves. The same pattern holds when a patient moves an appointment or a subscriber cannot log in after a charge they don't recognize. In each case, the agent picks up when the customer steps away from the app or website and needs an answer now, then hands them back to that same journey when the call is done.

Pulling that context together on a live call is the real challenge. It lives across many systems, the agent needs it in a fraction of a second, and it has to stay governed the whole time. That is where Databricks comes in.

A voice agent has two parts. The first is the conversation layer, which handles the call itself: carrying the audio, turning speech into text, and speaking the reply. Specialist partners do this well. In our prototype, LiveKit carries the call, Deepgram handles speech-to-text and the default voice, and ElevenLabs adds expressive voices. Phone carriers such as Twilio can bring in regular phone lines.

The second part is the brain, which Databricks provides. On every turn of the call, it looks up the caller’s context, applies your business rules, and chooses the next step, whether that means answering a question, making an offer, or handing the call to a person. It also records each decision so your teams can review it later. The conversation layer shapes how the agent sounds. The brain decides whether it gets the answer right.

The brain stands on a foundation of three things that already live together on Databricks.

  • Context is the data the agent needs at the moment: the customer, order, product, and policy data that belongs to the person on the line.
  • Ontology is how that data connects. It captures the definitions and relationships your business runs on, such as what makes someone a loyalty member, which store an order belongs to, and which policy applies to which product, so the agent can reason about your business the way your employees do.
  • Governance decides who can see what. On Databricks, an AI agent follows the same access rules in your enterprise data catalog that your employees already follow.

For Databricks customers, there is no new platform to stand up. The agent runs where your data already lives and connects to the systems you already run, such as ordering, loyalty, and CRM, through approved, read-only lookups.

During a customer interaction, the agent uses your context and ontology to look up this person’s orders, your policies, and your product information, so every answer reflects your business rather than general knowledge from the internet. The agent only sees the records that belong to the caller, and it confirms who they are by checking your systems rather than taking their word for it. Your business decides which offers the agent can make, how much credit it can give, and the point at which a person takes over.

If the agent cannot find the answer in your data, it tells the caller so and transfers them to a person rather than guessing. Every answer it does give can be traced back to the record it came from. Sensitive topics, such as medical, financial, or safety questions, are routed to a human by design, and the agent is built never to give medical advice. Only the conversation passes through speech partners, and customer data stays on your governed platform.

A voice agent needs two kinds of thinking. Some decisions have to happen in a fraction of a second, like whether a driver with a dock problem or an upset caller should go to a person right now. Others need careful reasoning, like working out the right fix for a delayed order. Researchers call this fast and slow thinking, or System 1 and System 2, and AI is now being built the same way. Large language models (System 2) do the careful reasoning, while a new class of fast decision models (System 1), such as Jev from TypeSafe AI, handles the quick calls. Databricks brings System 1 decision making to your governed data with ai_decide, so the agent can make a quick call and show how confident it is.

In a voice agent, the two work side by side on every turn of the conversation.

  • A loyal member or returning guest gets their full history and the offers they qualify for, backed by your most capable model, while a routine question gets a quick, accurate answer at lower cost.
  • An upset caller is handed to a person, along with the order or reservation, any earlier complaints, and any offers already made.
  • A caller who switches languages hears the agent switch with them.
  • A subscriber who sees a charge they don't recognize and can't log in is verified against your records and moved straight to account recovery, instead of waiting in a general queue.
  • A subscriber who calls to cancel hears the save offer they actually qualify for, at the moment it can still change their mind.
  • A patient who asks whether a symptom is serious is transferred to a nurse with the full transcript.
  • A driver reporting a dock incident is escalated immediately, before it costs you a shipment.

This lets you use your most capable models where they make a real difference to the customer, and faster, lower-cost models for everything else.

Every one of those decisions is recorded. With caller consent and recording disclosure handled at the phone layer, each call can be captured in one governed place: what was said, what was looked up, which model answered, and why each decision was made. Your teams control who can access those records and how long they are kept, using the same policies that already govern the rest of your data. The agent inherits the Databricks platform's security and compliance programs, including HIPAA and SOC 2 Type II options, described in the Databricks Trust Center. Speech partners carry their own certifications that need to be reviewed as part of your rollout.

That record is what lets the agent improve. Every call can be scored for quality automatically, and contact center and customer experience leaders can ask questions about their calls in natural language, such as why refund requests spiked last Tuesday. Those insights can then be fed back into better prompts and models, further improving the effectiveness of the voice agent.

Getting started does not require a large program. The building blocks are available today, and the Databricks Intelligent Voice Agents (DIVA) blueprint, which is open source on GitHub, gives your teams a working starting point. Voice then becomes a new channel on top of the systems you already have.

The voice agent is there to take on the routine calls that fill the queue, such as order status, refills, and rebookings, so your staff can focus on the conversations that need a human: an upset customer, a complex request, or a caller who would simply rather talk to a person. When a staff member picks up, the full history is already on their screen, and if anything goes wrong, the call moves to a person with the full transcript.

This is where customer service is heading. Gartner predicts that by 2029, agentic AI will autonomously resolve 80% of common customer service issues without human intervention, leading to a 30% reduction in operational costs.

Databricks industry engineers recommend starting with a 90-day pilot that covers one channel, one team, and your highest-volume routine call, such as order status, a driver check-in, or a supplier confirmation. Before the pilot begins, record today's cost per call, handle time, and customer satisfaction, and track whether callers come back and buy again, so you can compare the results at the end. Once the results hold up, you can extend the same governed setup to more locations and more types of calls.

Three questions for your next leadership meeting

  • Which customer and partner conversations do we handle most often, and which of them could an agent answer accurately today?
  • If a voice agent answered on our behalf tomorrow, would it know who it was talking to, and would it follow the same rules as our employees?
  • Can we trace every decision an agent makes on a call and show that it was governed?

To see it in action, watch the full demo and share the DIVA blueprint on GitHub with your technical team. It includes ready-made instructions that coding agents can follow. Then reach out to your Databricks account team to discuss and brainstorm your first use case.

Your customers will soon be talking to an AI agent on your behalf. What matters is how well that agent knows them.
